To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the larger the region, the more likely it will become the core in an economic geography setting; the more free trade, the more likely that the economically weaker region becomes the core; the more free international trade becomes, the more likely the relocation of industry will take place; and the larger the share of the ideologically non-neutral voters in the population of one country, the more protectionist the trade policy of competing nations.

(i) the larger region becomes more attractive as an industrial location as trade barriers are reduced, (ii) the equilibrium tariffs in a nation depend on the ideological distribution in its trading partners and (iii) the equilibrium trade protection can be higher under a majoritarian regime than under proportional representation.
the political economy of trade policy formation and retaliation, as well as the determinants of trade protection under different electoral rules are endogenous.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of political institutions on the equilibrium levels of trade protection.
the political economy of trade policy formation.
the effects of political institutions, such as electoral rules, on the formation of trade barriers and the location of economic activities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the equilibrium level and direction of trade protection is indeterminate.
electoral rules have a significant influence on trade policy outcomes, but the direction of this effect is not clear.
the type of electoral system does not have a systematic effect on trade policy, but that the effect is dependent on the distribution of voters across different districts.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the political power of voters in a country affects its trade policy setting behavior.
the political economy literature has made significant progress over the years, but there is still a need to understand the determinants of the political equilibrium in a more general setting.
we have shown how the equilibrium outcome of trade policy is affected by the distribution of voters’ preferences in the electorate and the structure of the economy.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, depending on the distribution of factor ownership among the electorate in swing districts, a majoritarian electoral system can be either more or less protectionist than a system of proportional representation.
the type of electoral system is not necessarily a good indicator of trade policy outcomes.
the political economy of trade policy can be better understood if the distribution of voters' preferences is allowed to vary across different types of electoral regimes.
